items.evidence: Found by this batch's node-path comparison on the command_parse run (the driver's compare() strips nodes, so this is invisible to the driver itself). Parse structure identical — same length, same positions — only the argument-name labels differ (vanilla names from the 26.2 datagen commands.json dump, confirmed by the oracle's live tree): /item replace block pos vs Rust targetPos (tree_misc.rs:174,190); /item replace entity targets vs Rust target (tree_misc.rs:172,188); /item replace ... from block source vs Rust sourcePos (tree_misc.rs:211); /execute if items entity entities vs Rust source (tree_execute.rs:230); /execute if items block pos vs Rust sourcePos (tree_execute.rs:237). 14 corpus commands show the difference; the /execute if items block row is invisible to the corpus because all 260 block variants fail on the slots sample (0 is not a valid slot) and failed parses carry no nodes — verified by code + dump instead. Parse behaviour on all 14 is identical (ok/cursor/error/suggestions agree); the names surface only in the tree's network form (the commands packet carries argument node names). Vanilla is itself inconsistent — execute if data uses source/sourcePos and execute store uses target/targetPos, both matching Rust. The 1.21.7 tree carries the same names, so this is a shared upstream naming choice, not a 26.2 regression. Fix is a five-name rename in the tree definitions.
items.method: command_parse node comparison + datagen commands.json + source
items.title: Argument node names differ from vanilla in /item replace and /execute if items

The remaining defects are small and peripheral: a dedicated-tree omission (/perf), dev-tree incompleteness, argument-name labels, and two still-broken oracles. The remaining risk is execution, not parsing: 19 of 22 drivers are unrun e2e drivers.
